title: Population screening that shifts unscreened lethal cancers to a curable stage

concept.text: The innovation would be a practical population screening program that finds cancers without effective established screening early enough for diagnostic follow-up and treatment to reduce advanced presentations, cancer deaths, or both. A multi-cancer blood test is one possible component. The capability belongs to the complete clinical pathway: detecting a signal, locating and confirming the cancer, and treating it in time to improve outcomes. Finding more cancers or achieving high assay accuracy alone would not establish this capability.

Conceptual clarification: the title describes the intended advance toward more treatable disease, rather than a guarantee that every screen-detected cancer would be curable. Earlier diagnosis does not necessarily change a cancer’s course, and late-stage disease is not uniformly incurable. The proposed innovation therefore requires evidence of better clinical outcomes within defined populations and cancer types.

significance.text: There is a substantial burden of cancer outside recommended screening programs. The supplied historical NORC report estimated that cancers without recommended screening accounted for 57% of cancers and 70% of cancer deaths in the United States. Those estimates motivate the proposed capability, but they do not establish current global proportions, how often these cancers first present through symptoms, or their stage at diagnosis.

Conditional significance: a screening program that demonstrably reduced advanced presentations across previously unscreened lethal cancers could substantially change oncology by allowing more treatment before extensive disease develops. A demonstrated reduction in late-stage incidence would directly mean fewer advanced presentations in the studied setting. A reduction in cancer deaths would be a further, distinct achievement requiring mortality evidence. If both occurred with acceptable harms, the program could shift part of cancer care toward preventing advanced disease from presenting.

Scientific interpretation: apparent gains in detection or survival after diagnosis can be misleading. Lead-time bias can lengthen the interval between diagnosis and death simply by starting the clock earlier. Overdiagnosis can add cancers that would never have caused illness or death. False-positive results can lead to anxiety, additional imaging and invasive procedures. These mechanisms explain why assay sensitivity, a larger number of early diagnoses, or longer survival measured from diagnosis cannot substitute for evidence that screening improves population outcomes.

Conditional downstream possibilities include less need for intensive treatment of advanced disease and a larger proportion of patients eligible for treatments intended to cure. Neither follows automatically from earlier detection: benefit depends on the biology of the cancers found, timely diagnostic capacity and effective treatment. Screening also does not itself eradicate metastases that already exist, so its impact remains distinct from a breakthrough in metastatic cancer treatment.

missing_breakthrough.text: The missing capability is demonstrated clinical utility for cancers without effective established screening: adding screening to usual care must reduce late-stage cancer incidence or cancer mortality with acceptable harms. The supplied NHS-Galleri trial establishes that a multi-cancer blood test can be delivered at population scale, but three annual screening rounds did not demonstrate a reduction in its primary stage III/IV endpoint across 12 prespecified cancer types. That result leaves the proposed capability unmet in this trial; it does not establish that every multi-cancer screening strategy lacks utility.

Engineering and clinical synthesis: a successful program must detect dangerous cancers during a window when intervention can change their outcome, while limiting false positives among people who do not have cancer. The supplied performance ranges show that very high specificity can coexist with incomplete cancer detection. The remaining challenge is therefore not simply to improve one accuracy metric, but to achieve a useful balance of detection, diagnostic burden and clinical benefit across the intended cancers and screening rounds.

Clinical-pathway synthesis: a positive blood result must lead to sufficiently prompt and accurate localization, confirmation and treatment. NHS-Galleri referred participants with positive results into NHS standard-of-care diagnostic pathways, illustrating that the assay is only the beginning of the intervention. Practical barriers include diagnostic capacity, access to treatment and avoiding workups whose harms outweigh the benefit of the cancers found. The supplied abstracts do not resolve which part of this pathway most limited the observed stage-shift result.

Scientific synthesis: the program must also distinguish cancers whose earlier treatment matters from findings that merely advance diagnosis or represent overdiagnosis. Screening interval, eligible population, cancer biology and follow-up duration all affect whether a detectable signal becomes a useful opportunity for treatment. Establishing that relationship requires clinical outcome studies; it cannot be inferred from analytical performance alone.

current_state.text: The supplied NHS-Galleri clinical-outcome report, published online on 22 September 2026 in the New England Journal of Medicine, describes an English trial enrolling adults aged 50 to 77. It randomized 71,122 participants to multi-cancer blood testing plus usual care and 71,128 to usual care with blood stored. These results document implementation of this particular screening strategy at population scale.

After three annual screening rounds, the incidence rate ratio for the primary endpoint of stage III or IV cancer across 12 prespecified types was 1.03, with a 95% confidence interval of 0.92 to 1.14 and p=0.63. The trial therefore did not demonstrate a reduction in that endpoint. The stage IV incidence rate ratio was 0.86, with a 95% confidence interval of 0.74 to 1.00. This separate estimate does not overturn the primary result or establish a mortality benefit. The null primary result does not prove equivalence between groups or exclude a benefit emerging with longer follow-up; the authors recommended further follow-up.

The companion performance report, published on 22 September 2026 in Nature Medicine, reports episode sensitivity across rounds of 26.7% to 37.2% for all cancers and 47.6% to 63.4% for the 12 prespecified types. Specificity ranged from 99.50% to 99.60%. These analyses were descriptive, without hypothesis testing. The figures demonstrate measurable detection performance and delivery at scale, but do not themselves demonstrate clinical benefit. They are not reported here as stage I sensitivity, and the trial’s 12 prespecified cancer types should not automatically be treated as identical to the cancers lacking established effective screening.

The clinical-outcome abstract reports trial-related adverse events in less than 1% of participants, with none serious. That finding should retain its stated scope: it does not establish the comprehensive absence of false-positive harms, overdiagnosis or burdens from diagnostic workup. The supplied abstracts do not report a mortality result.

The evidence available through the supplied review consists of retained PubMed abstracts for these two published reports, rather than the full research articles or figure images. The performance abstract was available intact in the reviewed material; an earlier account of a failed second retrieval cannot be verified from the supplied record and does not invalidate that abstract. No bounded search record was supplied to establish the status of the entire field as of 1 November 2026. The conclusions here therefore concern the dated NHS-Galleri findings and do not assert that every screening approach has been assessed or that later results are absent.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: a randomized population trial should compare screening plus usual care with usual care and show a clinically meaningful reduction in late-stage cancer incidence, cancer mortality, or both, for prespecified cancers without an established effective screening program. The population, cancer types, screening schedule, follow-up duration, effect-size requirement and statistical decision rules should be specified in advance. This is a proposed evaluation framework, not an established consensus threshold.
completion_criteria.label: Randomized screening meaningfully reduces late-stage cancer incidence or cancer mortality

completion_criteria.text: Proposed interpretation of success: a convincing late-stage reduction would satisfy the stage-shift component of this concept, while a claim of fewer cancer deaths would require mortality evidence. More cancers detected, higher sensitivity or longer survival measured from diagnosis would not qualify on their own. No greater-than-95% stage I sensitivity or specificity requirement is adopted: the supplied material establishes neither a basis for that threshold nor its historical provenance.
completion_criteria.label: Claims of fewer cancer deaths require mortality evidence

completion_criteria.text: Proposed harm and delivery requirements: evaluation should measure false-positive findings, invasive diagnostic procedures, complications, overdiagnosis and the time required to reach diagnosis and treatment. Acceptable tradeoffs should be defined before results are interpreted and considered alongside the absolute clinical benefit. Practical demonstration should include the ability to deliver the diagnostic and treatment pathway reliably in the intended healthcare setting.
completion_criteria.label: Screening evaluation measures harms and demonstrates reliable clinical delivery

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility and boundaries: confidence should grow through independent confirmation or replication across relevant populations and healthcare settings, with results reported by cancer type and important participant subgroups. Follow-up should be sufficient to assess persistence of benefit and delayed harms. Finite studies would establish demonstrated breadth within their populations, cancers, screening intervals and care systems; they would not establish universal effectiveness for all cancers or all people.
completion_criteria.label: Independent confirmation reports benefits, delayed harms, and demonstrated effectiveness boundaries

related_concepts.text: Roster-based comparison: CLM-07, “Reproducible eradication of metastatic carcinoma,” is the closest related entry. CLM-13 aims to reduce advanced presentations through screening and timely care; CLM-07 aims to eliminate metastatic disease once it exists. Better metastatic treatment could benefit people whose cancers are missed by screening or already disseminated, while successful screening could reduce the number needing such treatment. Neither capability establishes the other.

Roster-based comparison: CLM-09, “Curative in vivo genome writing beyond the liver,” concerns a treatment platform rather than population detection. If such a platform eventually produced effective therapies for relevant cancers, those therapies could contribute to treatment after screening, but that connection is conditional and is not established by the supplied evidence. Demonstrating a curative therapy would not itself demonstrate that screening improves outcomes.

Roster-based comparison: CLM-08, “Safe multi-tissue reversal of human biological aging,” operates at a broader biological level. Any effect of that capability on cancer incidence or screening benefit remains unspecified in the supplied material. CLM-13 retains a distinct clinical target: improved outcomes from a defined screening and care pathway for cancers without effective established screening. The other roster entries address separate disease-control, repair or replacement capabilities and do not need to be merged into this concept.

unresolved_issues: The supplied record does not establish broader field status as of 1 November 2026 or the existence or absence of later clinical-utility results.
Full research articles and figure images were not reviewed; detailed subgroup findings, diagnostic-workup outcomes and limitations beyond the retained abstracts remain unassessed.
Mortality outcomes and whether longer follow-up changes the clinical-utility conclusion are unresolved in the supplied abstracts.
The overlap between the trial’s 12 prespecified cancer types and cancers without effective established screening remains unspecified.
The effect size, follow-up duration, eligible population, cancer set and acceptable harm thresholds for a convincing completion demonstration still require operational definitions.
The supplied evidence does not determine which biological, assay, screening-schedule or care-pathway factors explain the unmet primary endpoint.
The historical provenance of the greater-than-95% accuracy suggestion remains unknown; no such threshold is adopted.
The NORC estimates are historical US figures; their applicability to current populations or other countries is not established.

brief.title: Screening that catches deadly cancers while treatable
possible: People could be screened for dangerous cancers that currently lack effective routine screening, then receive diagnosis and treatment early enough to improve their outcomes. A blood test could start the process, but success would depend on finding the cancer and treating it in time.
why: For people with these cancers, effective screening would mean fewer diagnoses after disease has become advanced, fewer cancer deaths, or both. More patients could receive treatment intended to cure, with less need for intensive treatment of advanced disease.

sources.showed: The NHS-Galleri trial delivered blood testing for multiple cancers across a large population in England. It did not demonstrate a reduction in its main measure of advanced cancer compared with usual care.
sources.quote: Less than 1% of participants had trial-related adverse events; none were serious.
sources.cited_for: The trial demonstrates large-scale delivery, but its main test of reducing advanced cancer was unsuccessful.
sources.not_established: It did not establish fewer cancer deaths or a complete account of screening harms.

sources.showed: Blood testing detected cancers and rarely gave positive results in people without cancer, but missed many cancers. These descriptive analyses measured test performance.
sources.quote: In aggregate, 937 participants had MCED-detected primary cancers.
sources.cited_for: The companion study shows how the blood test performed within the screening program.
sources.not_established: Detecting cancers does not establish that screening prevents advanced disease or saves lives.

shown: NHS-Galleri researchers have shown that blood testing for multiple cancers can run at population scale. After three annual screening rounds, their randomized trial, which assigned people by chance to screening or usual care, did not demonstrate fewer advanced cancers on its main measure.
missing: A program must demonstrate fewer advanced cancers or cancer deaths among people screened for cancers that lack effective routine screening.
Positive results must lead reliably to prompt diagnosis and treatment in the intended healthcare setting.
The benefit must justify false alarms, invasive follow-up and detection of cancers that would never have caused illness.

milestones.label: A randomized trial finds fewer advanced cancers or deaths
milestones.explanation: A randomized population trial would have to show a meaningful reduction for cancers lacking effective screening, using criteria set beforehand. This would establish that the program improves outcomes.

milestones.label: Fewer cancer deaths are demonstrated directly
milestones.explanation: A claim of fewer cancer deaths would require measured mortality, meaning deaths from cancer. Fewer advanced cancers could establish that benefit without proving that screening saves lives.

milestones.label: Benefits justify harms, and care reaches patients reliably
milestones.explanation: Evaluation would have to measure harms and delays through diagnosis and treatment against acceptable tradeoffs set beforehand. This would establish whether the whole program delivers worthwhile care.

milestones.label: Independent studies confirm lasting benefits and their limits
milestones.explanation: Independent studies would have to confirm benefits across relevant settings and groups, with follow-up for delayed harms and results by cancer type. This would establish where the program works and whether benefits last.

uncertain: Longer follow-up could change the NHS-Galleri findings; its effect on cancer deaths remains unresolved.
It remains unclear which features of cancer biology, testing, screening schedules or follow-up care explain the trial's main result.
The size of benefit, follow-up period and acceptable harms needed to judge success still require clear definitions.

page.title: Multi-cancer screening with reduced cancer mortality
page.definition: A population screening programme offers people without symptoms a single test for signals from several cancers. A positive result prompts investigations to establish whether cancer is present and where it is. Screening and subsequent treatment reduce deaths from a prespecified group of cancers that lack established effective screening, and the benefits of the whole programme outweigh its harms.

goal.need: A 2022 US analysis estimated that cancers without a recommended screening test accounted for 57% of diagnoses and 70% of cancer deaths. People with these cancers are usually diagnosed after symptoms appear. Earlier treatment could improve the chance of cure or spare some patients more invasive treatment. Testing for several cancers at once could extend screening to uncommon cancers for which separate tests would multiply costs and false alarms. The gain depends on effective treatment and must outweigh harm from unnecessary investigations and treatment.

completion.title: Multicancer screening reduces cancer mortality and its benefits exceed its harms.
completion.criterion: In a randomized population trial, deaths from the prespecified group of cancers without established effective screening are lower among people assigned to an offer of multicancer screening plus usual care than among those assigned to usual care alone. Follow-up starts at randomization and the comparison meets the trial’s prespecified statistical decision rule. Report outcomes for the cancer group as a whole and by cancer type. The benefits of the complete programme outweigh harms from false positives, diagnostic complications, overdiagnosis and overtreatment.
completion.set_by: US National Cancer Institute, Division of Cancer Prevention, clinical-utility definition for multicancer detection. UK National Screening Committee, population-screening criteria 11 and 13 and 2026 position statements on multicancer detection and surrogate outcomes.
completion.threshold_quote: fewer cancer deaths in the population of screened individuals compared to a control population.
completion.basis: NCI defines clinical utility by the difference in cancer deaths between screened and control populations. The prespecified group of cancers without established effective screening is the scope of this goal. The UK committee calls for aggregate and cancer-specific reporting to show which cancers contribute to benefit and harm. It treats late-stage incidence as an intermediate outcome. Neither body sets a universal percentage reduction or follow-up duration.

milestones.title: A multicancer blood assay distinguishes cancer cases from non-cancer controls in clinical validation.
milestones.criterion: Apply the blood assay to specimens from people with established cancer and from non-cancer controls. Estimate the true-positive and false-positive rates, or the curve relating them across decision thresholds, to assess discrimination. Assess reproducibility by repeating measurements on the same specimens within and between laboratories.
milestones.set_by: National Cancer Institute Early Detection Research Network, phase 2 of its adopted five-phase biomarker-development framework.
milestones.threshold_quote: distinguish subjects with cancer from those without cancer

milestones.title: A multicancer blood assay detects cancer in specimens collected before clinical diagnosis.
milestones.criterion: Test stored blood specimens collected before clinical diagnosis and compare them with specimens from controls followed for cancer occurrence. Assess how well the assay distinguishes future cases from controls as a function of time before diagnosis. Define the rule for a positive result before prospective screening.
milestones.set_by: National Cancer Institute Early Detection Research Network, phase 3 of its adopted five-phase biomarker-development framework.
milestones.threshold_quote: To evaluate, as a function of time before clinical diagnosis, the capacity of the biomarker to detect preclinical disease.

milestones.title: Prospective multicancer screening measures cancer detection and false referral in asymptomatic adults.
milestones.criterion: Screen asymptomatic adults prospectively and investigate positive results. Among all people screened, estimate the proportion who test positive and have cancer confirmed and the proportion who test positive and are referred but do not have cancer. These are the detection rate and the false-referral rate, respectively.
milestones.set_by: National Cancer Institute Early Detection Research Network, phase 4 of its adopted five-phase biomarker-development framework.
milestones.threshold_quote: detection rate and the false referral rate.

milestones.title: Three annual screens lower stage III/IV incidence across 12 prespecified cancers at two-sided p < 0.05.
milestones.criterion: Compare three annual blood screens plus usual care with usual care alone in adults aged 50–77 in England, with mean follow-up of 16–18 months after the third screen. The combined stage III/IV incidence rate must be lower at two-sided p < 0.05 across lung, head and neck, colorectal, pancreatic, myeloma/plasma cell, liver/bile duct, stomach, oesophageal, anal, lymphoma, ovarian and bladder cancers. Only if that test succeeds does the protocol test all eligible stageable cancers excluding prostate, then including prostate if the second test also succeeds.
milestones.set_by: NHS-Galleri investigators and sponsor GRAIL, published trial protocol, sections 2.5–2.6. This trial-specific endpoint includes cancer types with established screening.
milestones.threshold_quote: a statistically significant difference between the two arms in the incidence rate of stage III and IV cancers (p < 0.05).

milestones.title: Laboratory comparisons identify candidate biomarkers for a multicancer test.
milestones.criterion: Compare tumour and non-cancer specimens to identify and prioritize measurable differences that could be used to screen for multiple cancer types.
milestones.set_by: National Cancer Institute Early Detection Research Network, phase 1 of its five-phase biomarker-development framework.
milestones.threshold_quote: To identify leads for potentially useful biomarkers.

not_found: NCI, UK NSC and trial-protocol searches yielded no universal minimum mortality reduction, follow-up duration or numerical harm ceiling for multicancer population screening.
No published randomized multicancer-screening mortality result was located in the NCI and journal searches.
No NCI, UK National Screening Committee or American Cancer Society position was found opposing trials of multicancer screening for mortality reduction.

results.finding: Among 142,250 randomized adults in England, the stage III/IV cancer incidence rate ratio after three annual screening rounds was 1.03.
results.detail: The stage IV-only secondary endpoint had an incidence rate ratio of 0.86 (95% CI 0.74–1.00). The milestone is determined by the combined stage III/IV primary endpoint.
results.quote: The incidence rate of stage III or IV cancer (primary end point) did not differ significantly between the groups (incidence rate ratio [intervention vs. control], 1.03; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.92 to 1.14, P = 0.63).

results.finding: Of 303 NHS-Galleri participants with first-round results classified as false positive, 17.8% were diagnosed with cancer in later rounds.
results.detail: The post hoc analysis selected participants who had already tested positive, so it cannot estimate prediagnostic sensitivity or specificity in the screened population.

results.detail: False-referral percentages are calculated from Table 2 using all evaluable screens. The primary analysis used up to 12 months of follow-up per round. An exploratory review identified recurrent cancers among some referrals classified as false positive in the primary analysis.

results.finding: The targeted methylation blood assay had 51.5% sensitivity in the 4,077-participant CCGA validation.
results.detail: Samples were randomized across batches, operators, and reagent lots to minimize bias. The 95% confidence interval for sensitivity was 49.6% to 53.3%.
results.quote:
Overall
sensitivity across cancer classes and stages was 51.5%

results.finding: The multicancer methylation blood assay detected 95.1% of 81 cancer specimens in a 126-specimen analytical validation panel.
results.detail: The four runs varied operators, reagent lots and instruments. The cancer panel was selected to span high and low assay signals, so the observed detection fraction does not establish clinical sensitivity.
results.quote: Across four test runs with three groups of reagent lots and instruments, cancer was called correctly in 77/81 (95.1% concordant with diagnosis) cancer samples and 45/45 (100% concordant with diagnosis) non-cancer samples.

results.finding: PanSeer compared 200 tissue specimens and selected 477 differentially methylated regions for multicancer detection.
results.quote: We processed these samples using the PanSeer assay and identified a set of 477 differentially methylated regions (DMRs, see “Methods” section).

results.finding: PanSeer achieved 88% sensitivity in a held-out plasma comparison of 113 patients with established cancer and 207 non-cancer controls.
results.detail: Technical replicates were used in a pooled-plasma spike-in experiment to assess the analytical limit of detection. Repeat measurements of the clinical specimens within and between laboratories were unreported.
results.quote: The overall sensitivity of the classifier was 88% in the post-diagnosis cancer patients

results.finding: PanSeer achieved 95% sensitivity in held-out stored plasma from 98 future cancer cases, evaluated against 207 followed controls.
results.detail: The Methods give 98 held-out prediagnosis cases, consistent with the 191 total minus 93 training cases. The Results also cite 143 apparently healthy future cases without reconciling that count with the reported split.
results.quote: In these pre-diagnosis cancer patients, we observed an overall sensitivity of 95% in the leave-out test set

results.finding: INSPECTOR identified 4,229 candidate cancer-associated methylation regions using a discovery dataset of 6,342 specimens.
results.quote: We identified 4,229 cancer‐specific methylation regions that showed significant methylation changes in at least one type of cancer.

results.finding: The INSPECTOR blood assay achieved 81.9% sensitivity in independent validation of 824 participants.
results.detail: The study used replicate measurements of prepared DNA mixtures to assess the limit of detection. The criterion requires repeat measurements of the same clinical specimens within and between laboratories.
results.quote: comparable results in the independent validation set (99.0% specificity, 81.9% sensitivity).

results.quote: Among all cancers, detectability was 15.2%, 6.0%, and 2.3% for samples collected 1, 2, and 3 year(s) before diagnosis, respectively.

definition = "A population screening programme offers people without symptoms a single test for signals from several cancers. A positive result prompts investigations to establish whether cancer is present and where it is. Screening and subsequent treatment reduce deaths from a prespecified group of cancers that lack established effective screening, and the benefits of the whole programme outweigh its harms.". Reason: The definition omits the single test for several cancers and leaves the distinction between a screening signal and a diagnosis implicit.

goal.need = "A 2022 US analysis estimated that cancers without a recommended screening test accounted for 57% of diagnoses and 70% of cancer deaths. People with these cancers are usually diagnosed after symptoms appear. Earlier treatment could improve the chance of cure or spare some patients more invasive treatment. Testing for several cancers at once could extend screening to uncommon cancers for which separate tests would multiply costs and false alarms. The gain depends on effective treatment and must outweigh harm from unnecessary investigations and treatment.". Reason: The burden estimate establishes the size of the gap but leaves out how patients come to diagnosis, what earlier treatment could change, and why testing for several cancers together matters.

add statement by American Cancer Society workshop on multicancer early detection trials, The Peachtree Consensus, 2026: "the primary objective of cancer screening is to reduce cancer-specific mortality.". Reason: The Peachtree Consensus states the mortality goal specifically in the context of multicancer trials and explains why those trials also measure late-stage incidence.

edit completion: criterion = "In a randomized population trial, deaths from the prespecified group of cancers without established effective screening are lower among people assigned to an offer of multicancer screening plus usual care than among those assigned to usual care alone. Follow-up starts at randomization and the comparison meets the trial\u2019s prespecified statistical decision rule. Report outcomes for the cancer group as a whole and by cancer type. The benefits of the complete programme outweigh harms from false positives, diagnostic complications, overdiagnosis and overtreatment."; set_by = "US National Cancer Institute, Division of Cancer Prevention, clinical-utility definition for multicancer detection. UK National Screening Committee, population-screening criteria 11 and 13 and 2026 position statements on multicancer detection and surrogate outcomes."; set_by_kind = "government_programme"; threshold_quote = "fewer cancer deaths in the population of screened individuals compared to a control population."; threshold_ref = 4; basis = "NCI defines clinical utility by the difference in cancer deaths between screened and control populations. The prespecified group of cancers without established effective screening is the scope of this goal. The UK committee calls for aggregate and cancer-specific reporting to show which cancers contribute to benefit and harm. It treats late-stage incidence as an intermediate outcome. Neither body sets a universal percentage reduction or follow-up duration."; refs = [4, 3, 5, 16, 18]. Reason: The multicancer-specific guidance clarifies that the comparison includes everyone assigned to each group and that a pooled benefit can conceal differences between cancers.

add milestone after None: "Laboratory comparisons identify candidate biomarkers for a multicancer test.". Reason: The sequence starts at clinical validation and skips the network’s first phase, when laboratory comparisons identify candidate markers.

edit m1: criterion = "Apply the blood assay to specimens from people with established cancer and from non-cancer controls. Estimate the true-positive and false-positive rates, or the curve relating them across decision thresholds, to assess discrimination. Assess reproducibility by repeating measurements on the same specimens within and between laboratories."; threshold_quote = "distinguish subjects with cancer from those without cancer"; threshold_ref = 7. Reason: The criterion mixes CCGA’s observed accuracy with the phase 2 test of discrimination and reproducibility.

edit m2: criterion = "Test stored blood specimens collected before clinical diagnosis and compare them with specimens from controls followed for cancer occurrence. Assess how well the assay distinguishes future cases from controls as a function of time before diagnosis. Define the rule for a positive result before prospective screening."; threshold_quote = "To evaluate, as a function of time before clinical diagnosis, the capacity of the biomarker to detect preclinical disease."; threshold_ref = 7. Reason: The criterion gives PanSeer’s results but omits the phase 3 objectives of evaluating detection by time before diagnosis and defining a positive screen.

edit m3: title = "Prospective multicancer screening measures cancer detection and false referral in asymptomatic adults."; criterion = "Screen asymptomatic adults prospectively and investigate positive results. Among all people screened, estimate the proportion who test positive and have cancer confirmed and the proportion who test positive and are referred but do not have cancer. These are the detection rate and the false-referral rate, respectively."; threshold_quote = "detection rate and the false referral rate."; threshold_ref = 7. Reason: The phase 4 criterion needs the denominator for detection and false referral because the reported positive predictive value uses a different denominator.

edit m4: title = "Three annual screens lower stage III/IV incidence across 12 prespecified cancers at two-sided p < 0.05."; criterion = "Compare three annual blood screens plus usual care with usual care alone in adults aged 50\u201377 in England, with mean follow-up of 16\u201318 months after the third screen. The combined stage III/IV incidence rate must be lower at two-sided p < 0.05 across lung, head and neck, colorectal, pancreatic, myeloma/plasma cell, liver/bile duct, stomach, oesophageal, anal, lymphoma, ovarian and bladder cancers. Only if that test succeeds does the protocol test all eligible stageable cancers excluding prostate, then including prostate if the second test also succeeds."; threshold_quote = "a statistically significant difference between the two arms in the incidence rate of stage III and IV cancers (p < 0.05)."; threshold_ref = 11. Reason: The criterion mixes the trial result with its decision rule and leaves the later comparisons in the protocol’s fixed testing order unspecified.
